opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and I think the comparison with large language models is actually a bit misleading if you take it too literally.

With LLMs, the generality came almost "for free" once you had internet-scale text data. Everything humans write is already digitized, so you can pretrain one model and it suddenly can chat, code, translate, summarize. Robotics doesn't have that. Physical interaction data doesn't exist on the internet in the form we need — joint torques, contact forces, what happens when a hand slips on a cup. So expecting humanoids today to have LLM-level generality is unrealistic, and if you evaluate their economic value only through that lens, you'll be disappointed.

But I'd argue economic value doesn't require full generality. It requires sufficient generality within a scenario that's commercially meaningful. Think about a convenience store, a pharmacy, a warehouse picking station. The task space there is bounded but still very diverse — thousands of SKUs, different packaging, different shelf layouts. A traditional industrial robot can't handle that because it's programmed for one fixed motion. A humanoid with an embodied foundation model, even if it can't do everything in your home, can generalize across that entire vertical. That's already a big step change, and that's where real money is.

So my view is: generality in robotics will grow in a staircase pattern. First you get generality within one scenario, say retail picking. Then across a family of similar scenarios. Each step unlocks commercial deployment, and deployment generates real-world data, which feeds back into the model and expands the next step. That data flywheel is, in my opinion, the core of the business. The value isn't only in the robot doing labor today; it's in being the one that accumulates the data that makes the model more general tomorrow.

Another point — the way we've approached this is leaning heavily on synthetic data and simulation for pretraining, then using a smaller amount of real-world data for post-training. That's what makes the economics work. If you had to collect everything with teleoperation, the cost per skill would be enormous and you'd never reach scale. With sim-to-real, the marginal cost of a new skill drops dramatically.

And on the hardware side — why humanoid form? Not because it's cool, but because our world is built for humans. Shelves, doors, tools, all designed around human bodies. If you want one platform that can be deployed into many existing environments without redesigning them, the human-like form, or at least wheeled base plus dual arms and dexterous hands, is the most economical choice in the long run.

So to summarize: I don't think we should wait for "ChatGPT moment" generality before talking about value. The value starts when a robot can reliably handle an open-ended set of objects in one real commercial scenario, at a cost lower than human labor for that task. We're at the beginning of that now, and each scenario we crack expands the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response compares deployment cost with human labor, but does not identify a worker’s annual salary as a measure of a robot’s annual economic value.

r002.rationale: It explicitly argues that economic value does not require full generality and can arise from sufficient generality in a commercially meaningful scenario.

r003.rationale: The response discusses doing labor and beating human labor costs, but does not identify filling labor shortages as a source of value.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the comparison to large language models is actually the right place to start, because it clarifies what people are really asking. When they say humanoids lack generality, they mean a robot today can't walk into an arbitrary home and do an arbitrary task the way GPT can answer an arbitrary question. That's true. But I'd argue the economic value doesn't require that level of generality, at least not in the first phase.

Look at how language models actually started making money. It wasn't because they could do everything. It was because a handful of fairly narrow uses, like coding assistance and customer service, were valuable enough on their own to justify the whole stack. Generality was the long-term promise, but the near-term revenue came from a few vertical wedges where the technology crossed a usefulness threshold.

Humanoids will follow a similar logic. The question isn't "can this robot do anything a human can do," it's "are there enough tasks where a robot with 30 or 50 reliable skills creates more value than it costs." And in logistics, manufacturing, certain kinds of inspection and material handling, the answer is already getting close to yes. These are environments that are semi-structured, where the task distribution is narrow, where labor is expensive or hard to find, and where a robot running two or three shifts changes the economics fundamentally.

Now, why humanoid specifically, if we're just doing narrow tasks? Two reasons. First, the world is built for the human form. Shelves, doors, tools, stairs, vehicles — if you want a general platform that can be redeployed across sites without rebuilding the environment, you converge on something roughly humanoid. Second, and this is more important to me as a researcher, the humanoid form factor is what lets you accumulate data and skills that transfer. A specialized arm on a fixed base learns one thing in one place. A humanoid that learns to grasp, carry, and navigate in a warehouse is building a foundation that carries over to the next deployment. So even the narrow applications are investments in the eventual generality.

I'd also push back a little on the premise. Generality in robotics is going to be judged differently from generality in language. In language, the training data was essentially free and already existed. In robotics we have to generate it, through teleoperation, simulation, and real-world deployment. So the path to generality literally runs through these commercial deployments. The robots doing narrow tasks today are the data engine for the general models tomorrow. You can't skip that step by being clever in the lab.

Where I'd be honest about the risk: the hardware cost curve and reliability are still the gating factors. A model that fails 5% of the time is annoying in a chatbot. A robot that fails 5% of the time in a factory is unusable. So the near-term value is real, but it's concentrated in places where you can tolerate supervision and where the failure modes are recoverable. The companies that figure out that deployment loop, and not just the demo, are the ones that will capture it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether robots create more value than they cost and mentions expensive labor, but it does not identify a worker’s annual salary as a measure of a robot’s annual economic value.

r002.rationale: It says economic value does not require human-level generality and gives narrow applications as valuable economic opportunities.

r003.rationale: It identifies work sites where labor is “hard to find” as places humanoid robots can create value.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish generality from economic value. A humanoid robot doesn’t have to do everything a person can do to be useful. If it can reliably perform a particular task that people need done, at a competitive cost, that can already create value.

The key is to look beyond an impressive demonstration. How often does it succeed? How much human intervention does it need? How much does it cost to operate and maintain? A robot that works well for a few minutes but constantly needs assistance may have very little economic value. A robot with a narrower capability that works consistently could be valuable.

The humanoid form offers a possible advantage because our workplaces, tools, and environments are designed around people. But that advantage has to justify the complexity. If a simpler machine can do the same job more cheaply, then the simpler machine is the better solution.

So I wouldn’t assess humanoid robots primarily by whether they match the generality of LLMs. I would ask whether they can turn a useful physical capability into reliable, affordable work. Start with tasks where that equation makes sense, and expand as the capabilities improve.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competitive cost and operating expenses, but does not identify a displaced worker’s annual salary as a measure of the robot’s annual economic value.

r002.rationale: It explicitly separates generality from economic value and says a robot with narrower capabilities can still be valuable if it performs useful work reliably and affordably.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention labor shortages as a source of economic value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should distinguish generality from economic value. A robot doesn’t have to do everything a person can do to be useful. If it can reliably perform a few tasks that customers need, at a competitive cost, that can already create substantial value.

For example, consider moving materials in a factory. The question isn’t whether the robot can also cook dinner or hold a sophisticated conversation. It’s whether it can move those materials safely, consistently, and cheaply enough. You have to include the full cost: hardware, maintenance, energy, deployment, and any human supervision or intervention.

Compared with LLMs, robots face a harder scaling problem. Software can serve another user at relatively low marginal cost; physical work requires another machine, and failures can damage equipment or injure someone. So reliability matters enormously. An impressive demonstration doesn’t necessarily translate into a productive deployment.

The humanoid form is promising because our workplaces and tools are designed around human bodies. But that advantage has to justify the added complexity. If a simpler machine does the job better, it should win.

So I’d judge the opportunity task by task. Limited generality can still support a valuable business. Broader capabilities become economically meaningful when they increase utilization, reduce deployment effort, or let the same robot handle more work.

r001.rationale: It discusses task value and full deployment costs, but does not identify a replaced worker’s annual salary as a measure of annual robot value.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says limited generality can still support a valuable business when a robot reliably performs needed tasks at competitive cost.

r003.rationale: It does not mention filling labor shortages as a source of economic value.
